**Trustly cuts a quarter of its workforce in profitability push**

*The Swedish pay-by-bank firm is shedding 200 roles as it narrows its focus to profitable markets, marking a sharp contraction for one of Europe's most prominent open banking players.*

Trustly is cutting roughly 200 jobs, approximately a quarter of its workforce, as part of a restructuring aimed at reducing costs and concentrating on markets where it can achieve profitable growth. The move represents a significant retrenchment for a company that had expanded aggressively across European and North American pay-by-bank markets.

The restructuring comes at a moment of consolidation across the European open banking sector. Mollie completed its acquisition of GoCardless earlier this month, while several mid-tier players have struggled to translate transaction volume growth into sustainable margins. Trustly had previously reported growing pay-by-bank volumes but has evidently concluded that breadth of market coverage is no longer viable without a corresponding improvement in unit economics.

For the wider sector, the cuts underscore a maturing dynamic: the open banking payments layer in Europe is moving past the phase where growth alone attracted capital and patience. Providers now face pressure to demonstrate that account-to-account payments can be operated profitably at scale, not merely processed at volume.

*Sources: [Trustly slashes 200 jobs](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48460/trustly-slashes-200-jobs?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**bunq rolls out Wero across four European markets simultaneously**

*A simultaneous four-market launch gives EPI its first pan-European neobank integration, putting Wero in direct competition with iDEAL and card-based wallets on a mobile-first platform.*

bunq has launched Wero across the Netherlands, Germany, France and Belgium in a single rollout, making the European Payments Initiative's (EPI) instant payment product available to its customer base in all four markets at once. The deployment is Wero's first integration by a pan-European neobank, in contrast to the market-by-market approach taken by traditional banking groups.

Wero has been steadily expanding its reach since its initial launch, with Austrian banking groups joining earlier this year and the product going live in Luxembourg. Rather than relying on domestic banking relationships, bunq's rollout pushes Wero through a mobile-first platform whose customers are accustomed to cross-border functionality and digital wallets.

The EU's instant payments regulation, which requires payment service providers to offer instant euro transfers, provides regulatory tailwind. Consumer willingness to use Wero over established alternatives such as iDEAL and card-based wallets remains the central barrier in markets where those incumbents are deeply embedded.

*Sources: [bunq Wero Rollout spans Four Markets as Neobank Flexes Scale](https://www.financexmagazine.com/post/bunq-wero-rollout-spans-four-markets-as-neobank-flexes-scale) — FinanceX Magazine*

**Kenya proposes open finance legislation covering banks and mobile money**

*A new payments bill would give the Central Bank of Kenya power to mandate consent-based financial data sharing across banks and mobile money providers, extending the open finance model to one of Africa's largest digital payments markets.*

Kenya has introduced a payments bill that includes provisions for an open finance framework, granting the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) the authority to require licensed payment providers to share customer data with authorised third parties, subject to customer consent. The bill covers both banks and mobile money operators, bringing services such as M-Pesa into scope.

Section 29 of the bill allows CBK to direct a provider to enable data sharing for open finance purposes, a significant regulatory power in a market where mobile money dominates consumer transactions. The legislation defines open finance broadly, suggesting Kenya intends to move beyond narrow payment initiation use cases toward a framework that could encompass credit, savings and insurance data.

Kenya's mobile money ecosystem is one of the world's most developed, and the decision to bring it under a formal open finance framework, rather than leaving data-sharing arrangements to bilateral commercial agreements, mirrors the regulatory approach adopted in the EU's Financial Data Access proposal. The bill's treatment of consent and CBK's enforcement powers will be closely watched as a template for other African and emerging markets.

*Sources: [Kenya Payment Bill Lets CBK Order Data Sharing](https://khusoko.com/2026/09/23/kenya-payment-bill-open-banking-data-sharing/) — Khusoko | [New CBK Rules: Banks, M-Pesa could get greenlight to share users' financial data](https://www.pulse.co.ke/story/new-cbk-rules-banks-m-pesa-could-get-greenlight-to-share-users-financial-data-2026092318070533807) — Pulse | [New law to require banks and payment providers to share customer data](https://citizen.digital/article/new-law-to-require-banks-and-payment-providers-to-share-customer-data-n390698) — Citizen Digital*

**Banca d'Italia tells payment firms to screen both parties on all transfers**

*The directive tightens sanctions compliance for Italian payment service providers and crypto-asset firms, requiring dual-party screening even where EU instant payments rules create exemptions.*

Banca d'Italia has instructed payment service providers and crypto-asset service providers to screen both the sender and recipient of every transfer for sanctions hits, going beyond the minimum requirements set by EU law. The directive addresses a gap created by the instant payments regulation, which bars PSPs from screening both parties on each individual instant transfer but requires them to vet their own customers.

The Italian regulator's position effectively sets a higher compliance bar for firms operating in Italy. By requiring dual-party screening on all transfers, including instant payments, it imposes an operational and technical burden that may require PSPs to invest in faster screening infrastructure capable of operating within instant payment processing windows.

The move comes as European regulators are preparing for the Anti-Money Laundering Authority to assume supervisory powers. Italy's decision to front-run harmonised standards with a stricter national interpretation creates a compliance patchwork that cross-border payment providers will need to navigate. It also highlights the tension between the speed requirements of instant payments and the thoroughness expected in sanctions screening, a friction point that banks flagged to the AMLA earlier this year.

*Sources: [NEWS: Bank of Italy tells PSPs, CASPs to always screen both parties to transfers for sanctions hits](https://www.amlintelligence.com/2026/09/news-bank-of-italy-tells-psps-casps-to-always-screen-both-parties-to-transfers-for-sanctions-hits/) — Amlintelligence*
